lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.text: A database is an organised collection of related data; a DBMS is the software that stores, retrieves and protects it. Compared with plain files, a DBMS provides data independence (applications do not depend on physical storage), controlled redundancy, integrity constraints, concurrent multi-user access, security and crash recovery. The three-schema view separates the physical level (how data is stored), the logical level (tables and relationships) and the view level (what each user sees). Changing the physical layout without touching applications is called physical data independence.

lessons.title: Introduction to ER Model
lessons.text: The Entity-Relationship model describes data before any tables exist. An entity is a distinguishable thing such as a Student or Course, described by attributes such as name or roll number. Attributes can be simple or composite, single-valued or multi-valued, stored or derived. A key attribute uniquely identifies an entity within its entity set. An ER diagram draws entity sets as rectangles, attributes as ovals and relationships as diamonds. Modelling first helps agree on requirements with non-technical stakeholders before a schema is chosen.

lessons.title: Entities and Relationships
lessons.text: A relationship set associates entities, for example Student enrolls in Course. Cardinality constraints state how many entities can take part: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one or many-to-many. Participation is total when every entity must take part, for instance every Course must have an instructor, and partial otherwise. The degree of a relationship is the number of entity sets involved; binary relationships are most common and ternary ones tie three entities together. A relationship can carry its own attributes, such as the grade on Enrolls.

lessons.title: Convert ER-Model to a Relational Model
lessons.text: Mapping rules: each strong entity set becomes a table whose primary key is the entity key. A weak entity becomes a table containing the owner's key plus its own partial key as the primary key. A one-to-many relationship is implemented by placing a foreign key on the many side. A many-to-many relationship becomes its own table whose primary key combines the participating keys, together with any relationship attributes. A multi-valued attribute becomes a separate table that references the entity. Composite attributes are flattened into their component columns.

lessons.title: Relational Data Model and Notion of Keys
lessons.text: The relational model stores data as relations: tables with a fixed set of attributes (columns) and a set of tuples (rows). In the formal model the order of tuples is irrelevant and duplicates are not allowed. A superkey is any attribute set that uniquely identifies tuples; a candidate key is a minimal superkey; the primary key is the candidate key chosen for identification. A foreign key is an attribute set that references the primary key of another relation and enforces referential integrity. NULL represents a missing or unknown value and cannot be part of a primary key.

lessons.title: Introduction to Relational Algebra
lessons.text: Relational algebra is a procedural query language whose operators take relations and return relations. Selection (sigma) filters rows by a predicate; projection (pi) keeps chosen columns and removes duplicates. Union, intersection and difference require union-compatible relations. The Cartesian product pairs every row with every row, and a natural join combines rows with equal values on common attributes, equivalent to a product followed by selection and projection. Rename gives new names, and division finds tuples related to all values of another relation. Query optimisers rewrite these expressions into cheaper equivalents.

lessons.title: Data definition using SQL
lessons.text: Data definition language creates and alters structure. CREATE TABLE defines columns with types and constraints: PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES. ALTER TABLE adds or drops columns and constraints, DROP TABLE removes a table and its data, and TRUNCATE empties it quickly. Foreign keys can specify ON DELETE actions such as CASCADE, SET NULL or RESTRICT. Choosing precise data types and constraints pushes integrity rules into the database, where every application benefits.

lessons.title: Basic SQL query block and subqueries
lessons.text: A basic query block is SELECT columns FROM tables WHERE condition. DISTINCT removes duplicates, ORDER BY sorts, and joins combine tables on a condition. A subquery is a query nested inside another: IN and EXISTS test membership, ANY and ALL compare against a set, and a scalar subquery returns a single value. A subquery in FROM creates a derived table. Many subqueries can be rewritten as joins; prefer the form that is clearest and let the optimiser choose the plan.

lessons.title: Aggregate functions
lessons.text: Aggregates summarise many rows into one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) ignores NULLs. GROUP BY splits rows into groups and applies the aggregate to each group. WHERE filters rows before grouping, whereas HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Every selected column that is not aggregated must appear in GROUP BY. For example, average marks per course is SELECT course_id, AVG(marks) FROM result GROUP BY course_id.

lessons.title: Normal forms - Introduction
lessons.text: Normalization reduces redundancy and update anomalies by decomposing relations using functional dependencies. A functional dependency X -> Y means that whenever two tuples agree on X they also agree on Y. Redundant storage causes insertion, deletion and update anomalies. A relation is in first normal form (1NF) when every attribute holds atomic values. Armstrong's axioms (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity) derive all implied dependencies, and the attribute closure X+ is the practical tool for finding keys and testing dependencies.

lessons.title: Normal forms - 2 NF, 3NF, BCNF
lessons.text: 2NF requires 1NF and no partial dependency: no non-key attribute may depend on only part of a composite candidate key. 3NF removes transitive dependencies: for every non-trivial X -> A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute. BCNF is stricter: for every non-trivial X -> Y, X must be a superkey. Every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but converting to BCNF can lose dependency preservation, whereas a 3NF decomposition can always be both lossless and dependency preserving.

lessons.title: Index Structures
lessons.text: An index is an auxiliary structure that lets the DBMS find rows without scanning the whole table, like the index of a book. A primary (clustering) index is built on the ordering field of the file; a secondary index is built on a non-ordering field. Indexes can be dense (an entry per record) or sparse (an entry per block). They speed up lookups and range queries, but cost extra storage and slow inserts, updates and deletes because the index must be maintained, so index the columns that appear in frequent filters and joins.

lessons.title: B+ trees on Disks
lessons.text: B+ trees are the standard disk-based index. They are balanced, so every lookup traverses the same number of levels, and each node is sized to fit a disk block so the fan-out is large and the tree is shallow: millions of rows need only three or four levels. Internal nodes hold keys that guide the search; all data pointers live in the leaf nodes, which are linked in order, making range scans efficient. Insertions split full nodes and deletions merge or redistribute underfull nodes to keep the tree balanced.

lessons.title: ACID properties and operations in transactions
lessons.text: A transaction is a unit of work that must succeed or fail as a whole. ACID stands for Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions behave as if run serially) and Durability (committed changes survive crashes). Operations include begin, read, write, commit and abort or rollback. The classic example is a bank transfer: debiting one account and crediting another must both happen or neither.

lessons.title: Concurrency control using Locks
lessons.text: Locks prevent concurrent transactions from corrupting data. A shared (read) lock allows many readers; an exclusive (write) lock allows one writer and blocks everyone else. Two-phase locking (2PL) splits a transaction into a growing phase, where it only acquires locks, and a shrinking phase, where it only releases them; 2PL guarantees conflict-serializable schedules. Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit to avoid cascading aborts. Locking can cause deadlocks, which the DBMS handles by detection with a wait-for graph, or by timeouts and prevention schemes.

lessons.title: Recovery using undo logging method
lessons.text: A write-ahead log records changes so that the database can recover after a crash. With undo logging, each update first writes a log record containing the old value, and all changed pages must be flushed to disk before the commit record is written. On recovery, transactions with no commit record are undone by restoring old values while scanning the log backwards from the end; committed transactions need no action. Checkpoints limit how much of the log has to be scanned.

lessons.title: What is Machine Learning?
lessons.text: Machine learning builds models that learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules. In supervised learning, examples come with labels and the model learns to predict them: regression predicts numbers and classification predicts categories. Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data, for example clustering. Reinforcement learning learns from rewards through interaction. A typical workflow is to define the problem, collect and clean data, choose features, train a model, evaluate on unseen data, then deploy and monitor.

lessons.title: Linear Regression
lessons.text: Linear regression models a numeric target as a weighted sum of features: prediction = w.x + b. Training chooses the weights that minimise the mean squared error between predictions and true values. With one feature it fits a line; with many it fits a hyperplane. Ordinary least squares can be solved in closed form, w = (X^T X)^-1 X^T y, when X^T X is invertible. Assumptions include a roughly linear relationship, independent errors with constant variance and little multicollinearity. R-squared measures the fraction of variance explained.

lessons.title: Gradient Descent
lessons.text: Gradient descent minimises a loss function by repeatedly stepping against the gradient: w = w - eta * gradient(L), where eta is the learning rate. A learning rate that is too large overshoots or diverges; one that is too small converges slowly. Batch gradient descent uses all examples per step, stochastic gradient descent uses one, and mini-batch uses a small subset, trading gradient noise for speed. Feature scaling makes the loss surface rounder and speeds convergence. For convex losses such as linear regression's squared error it reaches the global minimum.

lessons.title: Logistic Regression
lessons.text: Logistic regression is a classifier despite its name. It computes a linear score z = w.x + b and passes it through the sigmoid 1 / (1 + e^-z) to obtain a probability between 0 and 1. A threshold, commonly 0.5, converts the probability into a class. It is trained by minimising cross-entropy (log loss), usually with gradient descent. The decision boundary is linear in the features. For more than two classes, softmax regression generalises the model.

lessons.title: Decision Trees
lessons.text: A decision tree predicts by asking a sequence of questions about features and following branches to a leaf that holds the prediction. Splits are chosen greedily to make child nodes purer, measured by Gini impurity or entropy (information gain) for classification and variance reduction for regression. Trees handle mixed feature types, need little preprocessing and are easy to interpret. Deep trees overfit, so limiting depth, requiring a minimum number of samples per leaf or pruning controls complexity. Ensembles such as random forests combine many trees to improve accuracy.

lessons.title: Overfitting and Regularization
lessons.text: Overfitting happens when a model memorises noise in the training data and performs poorly on new data; underfitting is when it is too simple to capture the pattern. The bias-variance trade-off describes this: simple models have high bias and low variance, complex models the opposite. Regularization adds a penalty on weight size: L2 (ridge) shrinks weights smoothly, while L1 (lasso) can drive some weights exactly to zero, performing feature selection. More data, simpler models, early stopping and dropout also reduce overfitting.

lessons.title: Model Evaluation Metrics
lessons.text: Accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions but misleads on imbalanced data. A confusion matrix counts true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives. Precision = TP / (TP + FP) says how many predicted positives were right; recall = TP / (TP + FN) says how many actual positives were found; the F1 score is their harmonic mean. ROC curves plot the true-positive rate against the false-positive rate across thresholds, and AUC summarises them. For regression use mean absolute error, mean squared error or R-squared.

lessons.title: Cross-validation and Model Selection
lessons.text: A single train/test split can give a noisy estimate of performance. In k-fold cross-validation the data is split into k folds; the model trains on k-1 folds and validates on the remaining one, rotating k times, and the scores are averaged. Stratified folds keep class proportions. Use a validation set or cross-validation to tune hyperparameters, and keep a final untouched test set for an honest estimate. Avoid data leakage: fit scalers and feature selection inside each training fold only.

lessons.title: Complexity Analysis
lessons.text: Big-O notation describes how running time or memory grows with input size n, ignoring constant factors. Common classes in increasing order are O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2) and O(2^n). We usually analyse the worst case, though average-case and amortised analysis matter too: appending to a dynamic array is O(1) amortised even though an occasional resize costs O(n). Compare algorithms by growth rate rather than by seconds measured on one machine.

lessons.title: Arrays and Linked Lists
lessons.text: An array stores elements contiguously, giving O(1) access by index but O(n) insertion or deletion in the middle because elements must shift. A singly linked list stores nodes with a pointer to the next; inserting after a known node is O(1) but finding the k-th element is O(n), and each node spends extra memory on pointers. A doubly linked list adds a previous pointer so deleting a given node is O(1). Arrays have better cache locality; linked lists suit frequent insertions at known positions.

lessons.title: Stacks and Queues
lessons.text: A stack is last-in, first-out: push and pop at one end in O(1), used for function calls, undo, expression evaluation and balancing parentheses. A queue is first-in, first-out: enqueue at the rear and dequeue at the front in O(1), used for scheduling and breadth-first search. A circular buffer implements a fixed-size queue efficiently, and a deque supports operations at both ends.

lessons.title: Hash Tables
lessons.text: A hash table maps keys to array slots using a hash function, giving expected O(1) insert, lookup and delete. A collision occurs when two keys map to the same slot. Separate chaining stores a list per slot; open addressing probes for another free slot using linear probing, quadratic probing or double hashing. The load factor (items per slot) controls performance, so tables resize and rehash when it grows too high. A good hash function spreads keys uniformly; worst-case lookup is O(n) if many keys collide.

lessons.title: Trees and Binary Search Trees
lessons.text: A tree is a hierarchy of nodes with one root and no cycles. A binary search tree keeps smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right subtree, so search, insert and delete take O(h) where h is the height: O(log n) if balanced but O(n) if the tree degenerates into a list. In-order traversal visits keys in sorted order. Self-balancing trees such as AVL and red-black trees keep the height O(log n) using rotations.

lessons.title: Heaps and Priority Queues
lessons.text: A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array in which every parent is less than or equal to its children (min-heap) or greater than or equal to them (max-heap). Finding the minimum is O(1); insert and extract-min take O(log n) by sifting up or down. Building a heap from n items takes O(n). Heaps implement priority queues, used in Dijkstra's algorithm and event simulation, and heap sort sorts in O(n log n) in place.

lessons.title: Graphs and Traversal
lessons.text: A graph has vertices and edges that may be directed, undirected or weighted. Store it as an adjacency list (space O(V + E), good for sparse graphs) or an adjacency matrix (space O(V^2) with O(1) edge lookup). Breadth-first search explores level by level using a queue and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Depth-first search goes as deep as possible using a stack or recursion and is used for cycle detection and topological sorting. Both run in O(V + E).

lessons.title: Sorting Algorithms
lessons.text: Comparison sorts cannot beat Omega(n log n) in the worst case. Bubble, selection and insertion sort are O(n^2), though insertion sort is fast on nearly sorted data. Merge sort is O(n log n) in every case and stable but needs O(n) extra space; quicksort averages O(n log n) with in-place partitioning but has an O(n^2) worst case with bad pivots; heap sort is O(n log n) in place. Counting sort and radix sort avoid comparisons and run in linear time for bounded integer keys. A stable sort preserves the order of equal elements.
